Nolan is trying to put you in the mind of Leonard. btw look at this youtube short me having the exact same guttural reaction to Nolan's editing style in his second film as I did with The Odyssey is straight up poetry. of course when i read about this film all i saw was "no but you dont get it thats the point." as long as Nolan grubs know that a device or an affect was intentional, they can go back to getting on their knees. i did not once feel that the jarring ass cuts elevated the gimmick of the film-- and thats exactly what it is, a gimmick. about 10-15 minutes (or less) into the film you realize what the next two hours are going to be: Nolan jerking himself off. no but dont you see... you can't trust anything. oh and when i show you how Leonard got here you're going to be AMAZED! it felt calculated and static, somehow a movie played in reverse felt linear. once you "get" the structure, the movie becomes less a "mindfuck" and more you waiting for Nolan to shove the cold spoon down your throat. every scene comes with a footnote and he expects you to react like this to every revelation. reads more like a bad puzzle than anything psychologically compelling. and per Nolan's work, the pathos is sterile, manufactured, and cold; any emotion or aesthetic is sacrificed for endless time debauchery. its just that compared to something like Tenet, the "mechanics" are ass.

I finally watched Memento and it is one of Christopher Nolan's weakest films. Firstly I like the idea of the film, it follows a man suffering from short term memory as he searches for his wife's killer and to help himself piece the puzzle together he makes use of photographs and notes to remember key details. Now this is a fresh idea and something I haven't seen before but the execution was lackluster. The story and editing of the film is non linear. The film drops us into major plot points and goes backwards a couple of moments before that point to show us the events leading up to that major story beat. My issue is how jarring this while watching because you're confused half the time. Something major happens and then you're in a completely different scene that seems unrelated. I understand fundamentally it's to have the user feel like Leonard the main character because he has short term memory loss and throughout the film finds himself in strange situations he has no recollection of being in, but for me it made the film feel disjointed and difficult to comprehend. And the film's structure doesn't help with character introductions or development because the film introduces a character that knows Leonard but as the viewer you only get context of how they met later on, which makes it difficult to understand characters' motivations and why they behave the way they do. Another issue I have are the black and white exposition dumps Leonard gives us; they are misplaced and the black and white filter feels out of place. If the purpose of the film was to make the viewer as confused as the main character I'd say Nolan did a great job. The only positives of the film are Leonard's monologues. Most of the film is spent inside Leonard's head and Guy Pierce does a great job portraying his confusion and the struggles of short term memory loss and having to rely on notes and other people which could easily manipulated which is another aspect of the film I enjoyed. As Leonard tries to find his wife's killer you notice how the notes he makes and the people he talks to are unreliable and how he has to discover the truth when he can't trust anyone or anything. I love Christopher Nolan but Memento wasn't great.

Christopher Nolan’s directorial genius elevates a linear narrative into a deeply entertaining one. By placing the audience in a constant state of disorientation at the start of every scene, Nolan masterfully forces us into the same fractured mental state as Lenny, keeping us thoroughly engaged. The awe we feel each time we piece together a clue—an ability Leonard is tragically deprived of—is brilliantly executed. We also see that the protagonist is constantly cautious about whom to trust. He suspects he is being used, and while this is true, the only proof he has to back his theories is the anecdotal evidence he has gathered himself. This is a puzzle we, the audience, are also trying to figure out for the majority of the film. Towards the end, we realize that he is indeed being manipulated: by Natalie for arguably pragmatic reasons, and by Teddy, who kills two birds with one stone by giving Lenny a purpose for living while also serving his own personal interests. Because of this shared confusion, the audience is led to believe that Lenny's truth is our truth. However, at the actual chronological end of the story, Lenny subtly reveals that he’s actively choosing to live for revenge. He desperately wants meaning for his actions, or in his own words: "I have to believe in a world outside my own mind. I have to believe that my actions still have meaning, even if I can't remember them." The true tragedy is not what he has forgotten, but what he actively chooses to bury. His inability to move on is not simply because he cannot make new memories, but rather because of his own active choice to forget the ones that don't fit his narrative. Teddy captures Lenny’s state perfectly: “So you lie to yourself to be happy. Nothing wrong with that—we all do. Who cares if there's a few little things you'd rather not remember?" This perfectly reflects the true message of the film: the choices Lenny has made since the incident are ultimately to blame. His willingness to lie to himself leads him to commit terrible tragedies just so he can live comfortably in a fabricated reality. He chooses to ignore everyone's warnings and run from the truth. Despite everything that is revealed, he willfully continues living in ignorance, perfectly punctuated by Lenny's—and the film's—final line: "Now... where was I?" before looping seamlessly back to the opening sequence.

OBRA MAESTRA Antes que nada, mis dieces a Christopher Nolan por sacar adelante un filme así, tan original e inmersivo que, por lo menos a mí, me ha mantenido pegado a la pantalla en todo momento. Si no quitas ojo y prestas atención a TODOS los detalles, esta película es una auténtica joya. Me considero una persona muy observadora, siempre intento que no se me escape nada, y esta película ha sido hedonismo puro. Es increíble como Nolan hace que sientas la ansiedad, el agobio, la tortura y la cárcel mental de no recordar lo que ha sucedido hace dos minutos, rodando la trama al revés. Esa manera tan única de meterte en la piel del protagonista y tan diferente de cualquier otra película: aquí no estás inquieto por saber qué pasará después, si no por qué ha pasado ANTES. Es como si te convirtiesen a ti en el enfermo durante dos horas, y ESO es lo que la hace tan brutal. Es cruda, es misteriosa y su estética me parece sensacional, así como las actuaciones, la fotografía y la voz en off. Todos los detalles y los giros están tan bien elegidos que no puedo sino apreciar y aplaudir el proceso creativo del auténtico rematado de la cabeza que ha ingeniado semejante puzzle. En el ámbito filosófico, moral y reflexivo de la película —película que, por cierto, sigue una línea similar a Shutter Island en su invitación al dilema moral, lo cual, al tener que darle al coco, me encanta— es curioso como los dos personajes, “Teddy” y Natalie manipulan al protagonista para conseguir lo que quieren, así como el protagonista se manipula a sí mismo y se cree sus propias mentiras… y tira para adelante, aun tras asumir la verdad, ¿o no? A destacar la genialidad de Joe Pantoliano —Ralphie en Los Soprano , actorazo de los pies a la cabeza, un virtuoso este señor— a quien tanto cariño tengo. También, por supuesto, a Guy Pierce, se da por entendido. Para que luego parezca que soy hater de Nolan. Reafirmo lo que dije en mi review de Tenet. Donde más brilla Nolan es también donde más flaquea, es como un vaso de agua que a veces se desborda (véase Tenet o la Odisea) y a veces se queda lleno a la perfección (véase The Prestige, El Caballero Oscuro o Memento). ¡BRA-VO!
